catalog_locator: Ch. 2 'Phonetics and phonology', section 2.4 'Stress', pp. 28-29 (Google Books); also section 1.5.1 'Phonology', p. 5; section 2.8 'Phonology of word classes' (c) Postpositions and particles, p. 46; 'Symbols', p. xix; p. 179 only as a search-within-volume excerpt
catalog_quote: 2.4 Stress. The primary stress falls on the last syllable of a phonological word. botani [bo̜ta'ni] 'stingray'; ima [i'ma] 'story'; shikata [tsʰika'ta] 'sour'. In (diachronically) complex words, the secondary stress falls on the last syllable of the first (historical) morpheme. hinomadini [hiˌnu̜madi'ni] 'daughter-in-law'; hidobadi [hiˌdo̜ba'di] 'son-in-law'. The words hinomadini and hidobadi are not synchronically segmentable ... The secondary stress falls on the final syllable of the historical morpheme hino ~ hido 'grandchild' in both cases, although a different number of syllables occurs after them in the two words. [pp. 28-29] ... There are no contrastive suprasegmental features (though neighbouring identical vowels can be pronounced as one long vowel [V:], resulting in distinctive vowel length in the surface form. ...) Stress is always word-final. [p. 5] ... Postpositions and particles can be monosyllabic, in which case they are enclitics, i.e. they form one phonological word with the grammatical word which precedes them. Since stress falls on the last syllable of a phonological word, enclitics are stressed, except when followed by another enclitic. [p. 46] ... á, é, í, ó Stressed vowels. Stress is only indicated on morpheme-final diphthongs and in Portuguese loans with unassimilated stress. In all other cases the last vowel of a phonological word is stressed. [p. xix]

new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress is fixed and non-contrastive: primary stress falls on the final syllable of the phonological word (which includes enclitic postpositions/particles, so a single enclitic carries the stress; with stacked enclitics the last one does).
new_statements.secondary_stress: In diachronically complex (historically compound) words, secondary stress falls on the last syllable of the first historical morpheme, e.g. [hiˌnu̜madi'ni], [hiˌdo̜ba'di], regardless of how many syllables follow (pp. 28-29).
new_statements.exceptions: Portuguese loans with unassimilated stress and morpheme-final diphthongs, where stress is marked with an acute in the orthography (p. xix); enclitic information-structure markers attract the stress from a preceding postposition (p. 179 snippet); an enclitic followed by another enclitic is unstressed (p. 46).
new_statements.domain_note: Domain is the phonological word = grammatical word plus following monosyllabic enclitics (postpositions, particles); examples are citation forms of nouns/adjectives. Author states there are no contrastive suprasegmental features (p. 5).
new_statements.identity_note: Dienst 2014 describes Kulina (Madihá of the Kulina ethnic group, mainly upper Purus and Juruá, Brazil, with data also valid for Peruvian Kulina); he treats Kulina, Deni (deni1241) and Western Jamamadi as a Madihá dialect continuum but the stress statement is for Kulina proper = culi1244. SIL 'Madija/Culina' works (Adams, Agnew, Boyer, Wright) describe the Peruvian Purus variety of the same language.

sources.citation: [no author] (1972). Silabario culina, con traducción al castellano. 101 pp.
sources.note: A pre-reading syllabary: pictured key words (book pp. 1-69), syllable-reading exercises (pp. 71-90) and a Culina-Spanish word index (pp. 91-100). Its only linguistic note is the one-page 'Ortografía Culina' (p. 4), which lists the 23 letters and describes s, ds, h and the aspirated double letters; it says nothing about acento/stress, and the orthography carries no accent marks on Culina words (a few index words contain an unexplained apostrophe, e.g. ttodi'nani 'puñada', jore'nani, ttai'tahi 'está pisada'). Nothing to set against Dienst 2014's word-final stress.
